## Introduction

This tutorial covers [Chapter 4: Exploring categorical data](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/explore-categorical.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You will learn to summarize one or two categorical variables with contingency tables and bar plots, to read row and column proportions, and to compare a numerical variable across groups.

### Exercise 1

You should be doing this tutorial in a repo named `exploring-categorical-data`. If you are not, create one and then connect to it.

Create a new file, `analysis.qmd`, with the title `"Exploring Categorical Data"` and your name as the author. In a bash Terminal, render it:

```bash
quarto render analysis.qmd
```

Open `analysis.html` with Live Server (right-click it in the Explorer → **Open with Live Server**) and keep the tab open. It refreshes on every render. Going forward, we will just tell you to "Render" when we want you to take these steps.

Create a `.gitignore` with `analysis_files` followed by a blank line. Commit and push. Use AI however you like.

If `show_file()` fails, it is probably because you have not yet loaded `library(learnr2)` in the R Terminal.

## Contingency tables and bar plots

We will examine the relationship between `homeownership`, which for the `loans` data can take a value of `rent`, `mortgage` (owns but has a mortgage), or `own`, and `application_type`, which indicates whether the loan application was made with a partner or whether it was an individual application.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that prints `loans_full_schema`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-1-test
#| echo: true
loans_full_schema
```

###

This larger dataset contains information on 10,000 loans made through Lending Club. The 55 columns do not fit on the page, so the tibble lists the ones it could not show.

### Exercise 2

Replace the code in that chunk so that it counts the loans with each value of `homeownership`. Render.

```{r}

```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-2-test
#| echo: true

  count(homeownership)
```

###

Loans from Lending Club are typically for small items or for cash, not for homes, so `homeownership` describes the borrower, not the loan. The levels arrive in capitals and in alphabetical order, while the book writes them in lowercase from no ownership to full ownership: rent, mortgage, own.

8,505 loans were individual applications and 1,495 were joint. This imbalance affects how we should plot them.

### Exercise 4

Start a new chunk that creates `loans` from `loans_full_schema`, with `homeownership` converted to lowercase and its levels ordered rent, mortgage, own. Print `loans`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-4-test
#| echo: true
loans <- loans_full_schema |>
  mutate(homeownership = str_to_lower(homeownership),
         homeownership = fct_relevel(homeownership, "rent", "mortgage", "own"))

loans
```

###

We will refer to this modified dataset as `loans`. Recoding a categorical variable changes its labels and order, never its counts.

### Exercise 5

Start a new chunk that counts the loans in each combination of `application_type` and `homeownership`, then spreads the result into a table with one row per `application_type` and one column per level of `homeownership`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-5-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  count(application_type, homeownership) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = homeownership, values_from = n)
```

###

A table that summarizes data for two categorical variables in this way is called a *contingency table*. Each value in the table represents the number of times a particular combination of variable outcomes occurred, so 3,496 is the number of individual applicants who rent.

### Exercise 6

Replace the code in that chunk with a bar plot of the number of loans at each level of `homeownership`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-6
#| echo: false

```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-6-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  ggplot(aes(x = homeownership)) +
  geom_bar()
```

###

A *bar plot* is a common way to display a single categorical variable. The bars appear in the order rent, mortgage, own because that is the order of the levels you set.

### Exercise 7

Change the bar plot so that it shows the proportion of loans at each level of `homeownership` rather than the count. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-7-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  count(homeownership) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = homeownership, y = proportion)) +
  geom_col()
```

###

Nearly half of borrowers, 47.9%, have a mortgage, while 38.6% rent and 13.5% own outright. The shape matches the count plot, and only the axis changed.

Replace the code in that chunk with a stacked bar plot: the count of loans at each level of `homeownership`, with each bar filled by `application_type`. Render.

###

This plot most clearly displays that loan applicants most commonly live in mortgaged homes. It is difficult to say, based on this plot alone, how different application types vary across the levels of homeownership.

### Exercise 9

Change the stacked bar plot so that every bar is stretched to the same height, showing the proportion of each `application_type` within each level of `homeownership`. Render.

```{r}
  ggplot(aes(x = homeownership, fill = application_type)) +

```

###

This is a *standardized bar plot*, also known as a *filled bar plot*. Since the proportions of joint and individual loans vary across the groups, we can conclude that the two variables are associated for this sample.

### Exercise 10

Change the plot so that the two application types sit side by side within each level of `homeownership` instead of on top of each other. Render.


```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-10-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  ggplot(aes(x = homeownership, fill = application_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

###

This *dodged bar plot* most clearly displays that within each level of homeownership, individual applications are more common than joint applications. When two groups are of very different sizes, as we see in the group `own` relative to either of the other two groups, it is difficult to discern if there is an association between the variables.

### Exercise 11

Replace the plot with a table of row proportions: for each `application_type`, the proportion of its loans at each level of `homeownership`, spread into one column per level. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-11-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  count(application_type, homeownership) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n), .by = application_type) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = homeownership, values_from = proportion)
```

###

The value 3496 at the intersection of individual and rent is replaced by 3496 / 8505 = 0.411, the proportion of individual applicants who rent. Each row now sums to 1.

### Exercise 12

Change the table to column proportions: for each level of `homeownership`, the proportion of its loans with each `application_type`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-12-test
#| echo: true
loans |>
  count(application_type, homeownership) |>
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n), .by = homeownership) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = homeownership, values_from = proportion)
```

###

Here the value 0.906 indicates that 90.6% of renters applied as individuals for the loan, against 80.2% of mortgage holders and 86.5% of owners. Row proportions and column proportions answer different questions.

### Exercise 13

Replace the code in that chunk so that it uses `email` to calculate, for each email `format`, the proportion of messages that are `spam`. Label the formats `"text"` and `"HTML"`. Render.

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-13

```

###

```{r}
#| label: contingency-tables-and-bar-plots-13-test
#| echo: true
email |>
  mutate(format = if_else(format == 1, "HTML", "text")) |>
  summarize(prop_spam = mean(spam == 1), .by = format)
```

###

A higher fraction of plain text emails are spam (209/1195 = 17.5%) than compared to HTML emails (158/2726 = 5.8%). Usually it is most useful to "condition" on the explanatory variable, here the format.

## Comparing numerical data across groups

We will revisit the `county` dataset and compare the median household income for counties that gained population from 2010 to 2017 versus counties that had no gain.

### Exercise 1

Start a new chunk that drops the counties with a missing `pop_change` or `median_hh_income`, adds a variable `change` equal to `"gain"` when `pop_change` is positive and `"no gain"` otherwise, stores the result as `county_change`, and counts the counties in each `change` group. Render.

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-1-test
#| echo: true
county_change <- county |>
  drop_na(pop_change, median_hh_income) |>
  mutate(change = if_else(pop_change > 0, "gain", "no gain"))

county_change |>
  count(change)
```

###

Of the 3,139 counties with 2017 population data, in 1,541 the population increased from 2010 to 2017 and in the remaining 1,598 the population decreased. Two of the 1,541, in Alaska and South Dakota, have no income figure, so 1,539 remain here.

### Exercise 2

Replace the count with a calculation of the median `median_hh_income` for each `change` group. Render.

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-2
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-2-test
#| echo: true
county_change <- county |>
  drop_na(pop_change, median_hh_income) |>
  mutate(change = if_else(pop_change > 0, "gain", "no gain"))

county_change |>
  summarize(median_income = median(median_hh_income),
            .by = change)
```

###

Growing counties have a median household income of $52,080, against $44,842 for the rest. While we might like to make a causal connection between income and population growth, remember that these are observational data.

### Exercise 3

Replace the summary with a histogram of `median_hh_income` from `county_change`, filled by `change`, with the two groups overlapping and semi-transparent. Render.

```{r}

county_change |>

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000, alpha = 0.5, position = "identity")
```

###

Color can be used to split histograms for numerical variables by levels of a categorical variable. Both groups are right skewed, and the gain group sits a little further right.

### Exercise 4

Replace the histogram with side-by-side box plots of `median_hh_income`, one for each `change` group. Render.

```{r}
county_change |>
```

###

The side-by-side box plots are especially useful for comparing centers and spreads, while the hollow histograms are more useful for seeing distribution shape, skew, modes, and potential anomalies. The gain group's box is wider: its IQR is $16,241 against $13,031.

### Exercise 6

Replace the ridge plot with a count of counties in each combination of `change` and `metro`, dropping counties with unknown `metro`. Render.

Most metro counties grew, 829 of 1,165, while most non-metro counties did not, 1,261 of 1,971. Growth and metro status are associated, so the income gap might belong to either one.

### Exercise 7

Replace the count with histograms of `median_hh_income`, one panel for each combination of `change` and `metro`, laid out with `change` in rows and `metro` in columns. Render.

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-7-test
#| echo: true
county_change <- county |>
  drop_na(pop_change, median_hh_income) |>
  mutate(change = if_else(pop_change > 0, "gain", "no gain"))

county_change |>
  drop_na(metro) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_hh_income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000) +
  facet_grid(change ~ metro, labeller = label_both)
```

###

In *faceting*, we split (facet) the graphical display of the data across plotting windows based on groups. An advantage of this approach is that it extends to splitting the data across levels of two categorical variables, which allows for displaying relationships between three variables.

### Exercise 8

Improve the faceted histograms. Show income in dollars, and add a title, axis labels, a subtitle that states the main finding, and a caption giving the number of counties. Render.

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question('In the R Terminal, run show_file("analysis.qmd"). CP/CR.', type = "reflection")
```

###

```{r}
#| label: comparing-numerical-data-across-groups-8-test
#| echo: true
county_change <- county |>
  drop_na(pop_change, median_hh_income) |>
  mutate(change = if_else(pop_change > 0, "gain", "no gain"))

county_change |>
  drop_na(metro) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_hh_income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000) +
  facet_grid(change ~ metro, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1 / 1000, suffix = "K")) +
  labs(title = "Median Household Income in US Counties, by Growth and Metro Status",
       subtitle = "Metro counties earn more whether or not they grew, and growing counties earn more either way",
       x = "Median Household Income",
       y = "Counties",
       caption = "3,136 US counties with known population change and metro status")
```

###

The medians run from $43,674 for non-metro counties that did not grow to $57,302 for metro counties that did. Adding `median_edu`, the book finds that regardless of the location or change in population, there is an increase in median household income from individuals with only a HS diploma, to individuals with some college, to individuals with a Bachelor's degree.

## Summary

This tutorial covered [Chapter 4: Exploring categorical data](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/explore-categorical.html) from [*Introduction to Modern Statistics*](https://openintrostat.github.io/ims/) by Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. You have learned to summarize one or two categorical variables with contingency tables and bar plots, to read row and column proportions, and to compare a numerical variable across groups.

Fluently working with categorical variables is an important skill for data analysts. In this tutorial we have introduced different visualizations and numerical summaries applied to categorical variables. The graphical visualizations are even more descriptive when two variables are presented simultaneously. We presented bar plots and estimations of conditional proportions.

For more on choosing among bar plots, read the "[Visualizing amounts](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-amounts.html)" and "[Visualizing proportions](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-proportions.html)" chapters of Claus Wilke's *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, by the author of **ggridges**.

Many sentences in this tutorial come from the chapter, used under the book's [CC BY-SA 3.0 license](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/).

````{verbatim}
---
title: "Exploring Categorical Data"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)
library(usdata)
library(ggridges)
```

```{r}
loans_full_schema |>
  count(application_type)
```

```{r}
loans <- loans_full_schema |>
  mutate(homeownership = str_to_lower(homeownership),
         homeownership = fct_relevel(homeownership, "rent", "mortgage", "own"))

loans
```

```{r}
loans |>
  ggplot(aes(x = homeownership, fill = application_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(title = "Application Type by Homeownership for Lending Club Loans",
       subtitle = "Joint applications are twice as common among borrowers with a mortgage as among renters",
       x = "Homeownership",
       y = "Share of Loans",
       fill = "Application Type",
       caption = "10,000 loans; Lending Club")
```

```{r}
county_change <- county |>
  drop_na(pop_change, median_hh_income) |>
  mutate(change = if_else(pop_change > 0, "gain", "no gain"))

county_change |>
  drop_na(metro) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = median_hh_income)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5000) +
  facet_grid(change ~ metro, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1 / 1000, suffix = "K")) +
  labs(title = "Median Household Income in US Counties, by Growth and Metro Status",
       subtitle = "Metro counties earn more whether or not they grew, and growing counties earn more either way",
       x = "Median Household Income",
       y = "Counties",
       caption = "3,136 US counties with known population change and metro status")
```
````

###

Row and column proportions can also be thought of as *conditional proportions* as they tell us about the proportion of observations in a given level of a categorical variable conditional on the level of another categorical variable.
